changes.before: Engagement surfaces what staff and communities experience, the analysis turns that into evidence about the system, and applied practice changes a specific decision with a specific owner. The program measures whether that cycle happened, not how any individual scored.
changes.after: Engagement brings staff and community experience into the work. Analysis examines those accounts alongside other evidence to understand the process, and applied practice develops a specific response with the responsible decision-maker. Review what was tried and what changed without scoring individual learners.

changes.before: Start before the decision is fixed, be honest about inform versus consult versus designing together, compensate participants, and report back what changed. Tribal consultation is a separate government-to-government route.
changes.after: Begin while choices remain open, explain whether participants are being informed, consulted, or invited to design with staff, and plan compensation through approved arrangements. Report what changed, what did not, and why. Tribal consultation follows a separate government-to-government process.

changes.before: Foundation, integration, then institutionalization, where equity is simply how the organization runs. This describes the division as a whole, never individual staff; you can follow it under One DSD planning and progress.
changes.after: Foundation, integration, and institutionalization describe proposed stages for division-level planning. Use them to examine how equity practices become part of routine decisions; they are not labels for individual staff or evidence that a stage has already been achieved.

changes.before: Engagement is voluntary, private, and non-shaming. Staff learn on their own time, reflect without being recorded, and are never scored or profiled. That is why participation classes are labeled on every experience.
changes.after: Learning and reflection in this program are voluntary. Staff can choose a pace and starting point that fit their needs. Personal learning is not used to score or profile staff. Some activities let you save notes on your device; check the privacy information for the activity and keep identifying information out of shared work.

changes.before: Question what is treated as immovable. Approval bottlenecks, diffuse decision rights, credential gatekeeping, and legacy data built for billing are choices someone made and can remake.
changes.after: Examine approval bottlenecks, unclear decision rights, credential requirements, and data systems built for billing. Ask which features reflect necessary requirements, which are inherited practices, and who has authority to consider a change.

changes.before: Distinguish unfamiliarity from intentional harm, and distinguish individual conduct, which belongs in a confidential HR channel, from a systemic pattern, which belongs in the equity practice.
changes.after: Respond to reported harm without deciding in advance whether it was intentional. Use the appropriate Human Resources or other established channel for an individual concern and explain its privacy limits. A concern may also reveal a wider pattern, but equity analysis does not replace the formal process.

changes.before: Accessibility, language access, and plain language are default practices with owners, not accommodations granted on request.
changes.after: Build accessibility, language access, and plain language into routine work, with responsibility for implementation. Individual accommodation requests still need the appropriate established process; accessible design does not replace that responsibility.

changes.before: Change is staged from foundation to integration to institutionalization, and it is funded, staffed, and reviewed rather than only stated.
changes.after: Use the proposed stages of foundation, integration, and institutionalization to plan the work. Identify the resources, responsible people, and review needed at each stage rather than treating a stated intention as an implemented change.
